chapters.title: Chapter 5: Behavioral Economics in Organizations and the Workplace

lessons.title: Why Employees Don't Save Enough: Designing Better Retirement Defaults at Work

children.text: A Head of HR at a mid-sized Indian company pulls up the numbers before a benefits review: fewer than 3% of employees have ever opted into Voluntary Provident Fund, even though it offers a better, tax-advantaged, guaranteed return than almost anything else on the table. Every earlier lesson in this course looked at defaults from the person's side of the decision. This lesson flips the desk around. If you were the one designing this company's retirement benefits, what would the evidence actually tell you to do differently, beyond just noticing that defaults are powerful?

body.text: Retirement under-saving is not primarily a financial-literacy problem an HR team can educate its way out of. It is a choice-architecture problem, and the research on which specific design choices actually move outcomes is now detailed enough that a benefits team can follow evidence rather than guess.

children.text: The Employer's Version of the Same Default Effect

Chapter 2 covered Madrian and Shea's finding that switching a retirement plan from opt-in to automatic enrollment with opt-out lifted participation from roughly 37% to roughly 86%, without changing the plan itself. For an HR team, that result isn't a fact to know, it's a decision to make: whether new hires are enrolled by default into any voluntary savings option beyond the statutory minimum, or whether that option sits behind a form most people will never actively open. Nearly every organization already makes this decision, usually by accident, simply by however the onboarding paperwork happens to be structured.
Auto-Enrollment Is Necessary But Not Sufficient: The Default Rate Matters Too

Here's the subtler trap a benefits team can walk straight into. Auto-enrollment raises participation dramatically, but the same default effect also makes whatever contribution rate is chosen at enrollment sticky. If a company auto-enrolls new hires into a voluntary top-up at a conservative default, employees tend to stay at that rate for years, often for their entire tenure, regardless of what they would have picked if actively deciding fresh each year. Auto-enrollment at a low, never-revisited rate can genuinely leave employees under-saved for decades, precisely because it looks like the problem has already been solved.

body.yAxisLabel: ₹ lakh, corpus at 8% assumed annual return

body.text: This chart holds annual contribution constant, ignoring salary growth, purely to isolate the effect of the default rate itself. On even this simplified, illustrative basis, a 4-percentage-point gap in the default rate compounds into roughly a ₹45 lakh difference after 30 years. The default an employee never actively chose is doing more to determine their retirement outcome than almost any investment decision they will ever consciously make.

children.text: Chapter 2 introduced Thaler and Benartzi's 2004 Save More Tomorrow program as a footnote. For a benefits team, it is the actual design answer to the chart above. The mechanism only works because of three specific implementation choices, each worth copying deliberately rather than approximately. First, the increase is tied to future pay raises, not to current salary, so it never registers as a felt pay cut, sidestepping loss aversion almost entirely. Second, it is opt-out, not opt-in, at each future increase, so the same default effect that got someone enrolled keeps working at every subsequent raise. Third, well-designed versions include a cap, an upper limit past which contributions stop auto-escalating, so an employee is never auto-escalated into a contribution rate that would genuinely strain their take-home pay without a fresh, active decision.
Employer Matching: A Nudge, or an Incentive?

Run employer matching through this course's own nudge-versus-incentive test, and it's clearly not a nudge, it directly changes the economics: money the employer only pays if the employee contributes enough to trigger it. What is still a design choice is how the match gets communicated. Studies of employer-matched retirement plans have repeatedly found a meaningful share of employees contribute below the level needed to capture their full match, leaving guaranteed, risk-free money unclaimed, the workplace equivalent of the coupon nobody redeems. Framing an under-contribution as a specific rupee amount "left on the table" is loss framing from Chapter 3, applied honestly here, since the money really is being forfeited, not manufactured urgency dressed up as a loss.

body.title: Price the unclaimed match
body.prompt: A company matches employee NPS contributions rupee-for-rupee, up to 5% of salary. Priya earns ₹9,00,000 a year and currently contributes only 3% of her salary to NPS. How much employer match money is she leaving unclaimed each year by not contributing the full 5%?
body.explanation: Priya is matched only on the 3% she contributes. The unclaimed 2% gap × ₹9,00,000 = ₹18,000 a year in employer money she never receives, purely because her own contribution falls short of the match threshold, not because the benefit doesn't exist.

children.text: What This Looks Like in an Indian Workplace

markDefs.definition: A provision of the Income-tax Act, 1961 allowing an employer's contribution to an employee's NPS account, up to specified limits, to be claimed as a tax deduction separately from the ₹1.5 lakh Section 80C cap.

children.text: Many Indian employers now offer an employer NPS contribution under

as part of flexible-benefits or CTC restructuring, a genuinely valuable, tax-efficient option that, unlike EPF, almost always requires the employee to actively opt in and restructure their salary to access it. Predictably, uptake tends to be low wherever it's offered as a buried form rather than a presented default. A benefits team applying this lesson would build it into the onboarding and annual appraisal flow directly, present a sensible contribution level as the starting point rather than ₹0, and time any auto-escalation step to land alongside the appraisal cycle, exactly the raise-linked timing Save More Tomorrow depends on.

body.caption: Design choices for a workplace retirement default

cells: Set once at hiring, never revisited
Auto-escalated, tied to pay raises, with a cap
Mentioned once in a benefits handbook
Framed as a specific rupee amount left unclaimed if under-contributed
Available only if the employee separately requests it
Presented as a default option at onboarding and appraisal time

body.title: Should HR raise the default rate?
body.scenario: The HR head from the opening of this lesson is considering auto-enrolling all new hires into a 10% voluntary top-up, well above the company's current unused opt-in default, with a clear opt-out available at any time. A colleague raises a concern: "Isn't it a bit paternalistic to decide for people how much of their own salary to save?"
body.prompt: Using Chapter 1's responsible choice architect's checklist, how would you respond to this concern, and would you recommend proceeding?
body.modelAnswer:
1. Every original option remains genuinely available: the opt-out is real and low-friction, so no employee is prevented from choosing 0% if that's truly their preference.
2. The real economics don't change for the company or the employee's actual pay, only the default outcome absent action changes, which is the first two checklist items from Chapter 1 satisfied.
3. The whose-interest test matters most here: a 10% default clearly serves the employee's own long-run financial security rather than the company's short-term interest, unlike a sludge-style default such as an auto-added insurance add-on.
4. The one genuine caution is the default rate itself, it shouldn't be set so high that opting out becomes the only realistic choice for lower-income employees managing tight monthly cash flow, which is exactly why Save More Tomorrow-style caps and pairing increases with raises, not flat increases to current pay, matter as much as the auto-enrollment decision itself. With those safeguards in place, proceeding is defensible paternalism, not an overreach.

body.title: Auto-enrollment or auto-escalation?
body.question: A company already auto-enrolls every new hire into a 6% voluntary retirement contribution by default. Two years later, contribution rates still sit at exactly 6% for almost everyone, even employees who have since received two raises. Which specific design gap does this reveal?
options: A lack of auto-enrollment, since participation itself must be the problem
A lack of auto-escalation, since the default contribution rate was never designed to increase over time
A lack of employer matching, since there is no incentive to contribute more
The endowment effect, since employees feel they already own their 6% rate
body.explanation: Participation isn't the issue here, auto-enrollment already solved that. The rate itself never moves, which is precisely the gap auto-escalation, not auto-enrollment or matching, is designed to close.

body.title: Name the design fix
body.textWithBlank: Automatically increasing an employee's retirement contribution rate over time, typically tied to future pay raises rather than current salary, is called auto-___.
body.explanation: Auto-escalation, the mechanism behind Thaler and Benartzi's Save More Tomorrow program, specifically targets the sticky-default-rate problem that auto-enrollment alone doesn't solve.

body.title: How common is leaving employer match money unclaimed?

children.text: Research on US employer-matched 401(k) plans, the retirement system most extensively studied in this literature, has repeatedly found a meaningful share of eligible employees contribute below the threshold needed to capture their full match, effectively forfeiting free, risk-free money every pay cycle. The usual explanations line up with concepts already covered in this course: present bias making a slightly higher current contribution feel costlier than a guaranteed future match feels valuable, and a default contribution rate, often set well below the match threshold, that nobody revisits once selected. The fix employers increasingly use is not more employee education about the match's value, but simply setting the auto-enrollment default at or near the match threshold itself, so capturing the full match becomes the path of least resistance rather than a separate decision an employee has to remember to make.

body.label: The cost of a 4-point gap in the default rate
body.context: Illustrative 30-year difference between a 6% and a 10% contribution rate on a ₹10 lakh salary at an assumed 8% annual return, holding salary constant, purely from where the default was set.

cards.definition: The tendency for whatever contribution rate is set at auto-enrollment to persist for years, even as an employee's salary and circumstances change.
Automatically increasing a contribution rate over time, typically tied to pay raises and capped at an upper limit, to fix the sticky-default-rate problem.
A genuine economic incentive, not a nudge, where an employer contributes additional money contingent on the employee's own contribution reaching a threshold.
The Income-tax Act, 1961 provision allowing an employer's NPS contribution to be deducted separately from the ₹1.5 lakh Section 80C cap, commonly offered via flexible-benefits restructuring in India.
Contributing below the threshold needed to capture a full employer match, forfeiting free, risk-free money, usually because the default contribution rate sits below that threshold.

points: Auto-enrollment fixes participation, but the same default effect makes the chosen contribution rate sticky too, so a low, never-revisited default can leave employees under-saved for decades even while participation looks solved.

Auto-escalation, tied to future pay raises rather than current salary and capped at an upper limit, is the specific, evidence-based fix for the sticky-default-rate problem, not a vague call for more employee education.

Employer matching is a genuine economic incentive rather than a nudge, but how it's communicated is still a design choice, and honest loss framing, showing the exact rupee amount forfeited, addresses a well-documented pattern of employees under-contributing relative to their match threshold.

In India, NPS employer contributions under Section 80CCD(2) usually require active employee opt-in, unlike EPF, which is exactly why uptake stays low unless a benefits team deliberately builds it into onboarding and appraisal defaults rather than leaving it as a request-only option.

None of this requires removing any employee's choice. A responsible design, checked against Chapter 1's choice-architect checklist, keeps every option available while simply changing what happens if nobody actively decides.
